$$\mathrm{IG}(D,A)=E(D)-\sum_{v}\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}\,E(D_v)$$

Classification beyond a straight line: nearest neighbours and decision trees

Two ways to classify without one global boundary. Let the nearest training points vote, or ask a short sequence of questions. Each has a single knob — the number of neighbours, the depth of the tree — that moves it between memorising the data and ignoring it.

k-nearest neighbours Decision trees Gini, entropy & information gain ID3 and pruning

Part A
k-nearest neighbours
1

From one global rule to many local ones

Every classifier so far has searched for a single rule that holds across the whole feature space. k-NN gives that up and decides each case by looking only at its surroundings.

The two classifiers from the previous lecture both draw one straight boundary — a hyperplane — through the entire feature space:

  • Perceptron. Predicts \(\hat y = \operatorname{sign}\!\left(w^{\top}x + b\right)\). The boundary is the hyperplane \(w^{\top}x + b = 0\).
  • Logistic regression. Models the probability of the positive class, and thresholds it at \(0.5\).
$$P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma\!\left(w^{\top}x+b\right)$$ $$\hat y = 1 \iff \sigma\!\left(w^{\top}x+b\right)\ge 0.5 \iff w^{\top}x+b \ge 0$$

Deciding locally instead

A hyperplane fails whenever the classes are arranged in bands, rings, or islands. Instead of searching for a better global separator, k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) asks a local question: what are the labels of the training points closest to this one?

Class A
Class B
Failed Hyperplane
k-NN Local Check

Bands

Straight line mixes classes. k-NN identifies the local middle band.

Rings

Line bisects the circles. k-NN accurately scopes the outer perimeter.

Islands

Line separates the islands from each other. k-NN groups each island correctly.

The assumption behind it is a smoothness assumption: similar inputs are likely to have similar outputs. If that holds, the neighbourhood of a new point is a good guide to its label, and the shape of the overall decision boundary never has to be written down.

This makes k-NN different in kind from the perceptron and logistic regression:

Perceptron / logistic regressionk-NN
ModelParametric: a fixed number of weights \(w, b\)Non-parametric: the training set itself is the model
TrainingOptimise the weights, then discard the dataStore the data; nothing is optimised ("lazy" learning)
PredictionOne dot product, \(O(d)\)Compare against every stored point, \(O(md)\)
BoundaryA single hyperplaneAny shape the data supports
"Learns local structure"

The decision boundary adapts to whatever structure the data has, without anyone specifying a transformation. But no parameters are fitted and no summary of the data is produced — the "learning" is simply remembering. This is why k-NN is called an instance-based or memory-based method.

Is k-NN a linear classifier?

No. For 1-NN, the boundary between two training points of different classes is a piece of their perpendicular bisector, so the overall boundary is piecewise linear — made of many straight segments — and can enclose islands of one class inside another. As \(k\) grows the pieces multiply and the boundary looks smoother, but it is never a single hyperplane unless the data happens to force one.

2

The k-NN algorithm

Three inputs, five steps, and one voting rule.

Inputs

InputNotationMeaning
Training set\(D=\{(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),\dots,(x_m,y_m)\}\)\(m\) labelled examples, with \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y_i\in\{1,2,\dots,C\}\)
Test point\(x_{\text{test}}\in\mathbb{R}^d\)The point to be classified
Number of neighbours\(k\)A hyperparameter, with \(1\le k\le m\)

Steps

  1. Compute distances. For every training sample \(i=1,2,\dots,m\), compute \(d_i=\operatorname{dist}\!\left(x_{\text{test}},\,x_i\right)\), for example the Euclidean distance \(\lVert x_{\text{test}}-x_i\rVert_2\).
  2. Sort. Order the training samples by increasing \(d_i\).
  3. Pick the neighbours. Keep the first \(k\). Their indices form the set \(N_k(x_{\text{test}})\) of the \(k\) training points closest to \(x_{\text{test}}\).
  4. Vote. Count how many of those \(k\) neighbours belong to each class.
  5. Assign the label with the highest count:
$$\hat y \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\,\in\,\{1,2,\dots,C\}} \;\sum_{i\,\in\, N_k(x_{\text{test}})} \mathbf{1}\!\left[y_i=c\right]$$

The indicator \(\mathbf{1}[y_i=c]\) is \(1\) when neighbour \(i\) has label \(c\) and \(0\) otherwise, so the sum is simply the number of votes for class \(c\).

What is \(N_k(x_{\text{test}})\)?

\(N_k(x_{\text{test}})\) is the set of the \(k\) nearest neighbours of \(x_{\text{test}}\). Strictly, it holds the indices \(i\) of the \(k\) training points closest to \(x_{\text{test}}\). The \(N\) stands for "neighbourhood", and the subscript \(k\) says how many neighbours it contains.

Written out, sort the distances \(d_i=\operatorname{dist}(x_{\text{test}},x_i)\) from smallest to largest, and \(N_k(x_{\text{test}})\) is the set of indices of the first \(k\):

$$N_k(x_{\text{test}})=\{\,i : d_i \text{ is among the } k \text{ smallest distances}\,\},\qquad \lvert N_k(x_{\text{test}})\rvert=k$$

So \(\sum_{i\in N_k(x_{\text{test}})}\) means "add up only over those \(k\) neighbours", not over all \(m\) training points. For each class \(c\), the sum counts how many of the \(k\) neighbours have label \(c\), and \(\arg\max\) picks the class with the most votes.

If two points are tied for the \(k\)-th smallest distance, \(N_k\) isn't uniquely defined, and an implementation has to pick one of them by some rule.

Ties

The \(\arg\max\) can have more than one winner. With two classes an odd \(k\) rules this out; with \(C\ge 3\) classes it does not (three neighbours, three different labels). Distances can also tie, so that the \(k\)-th neighbour is not unique. Common tie-breaking rules are: shrink \(k\) by one and vote again, take the label of the single nearest neighbour, pick at random, or weight the votes by distance so that exact ties become unlikely.

Two useful variants

Distance-weighted k-NN. A neighbour right next to the test point is better evidence than one at the edge of the neighbourhood. Weighting each vote by an inverse distance captures this:

$$\hat y=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c}\sum_{i\in N_k(x_{\text{test}})} w_i\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[y_i=c\right],\qquad w_i=\frac{1}{d_i}\ \text{ or }\ \frac{1}{d_i^{\,2}}$$

If some \(d_i=0\) the test point coincides with a training point, and its label is normally returned directly.

k-NN regression. When \(y\) is a real number, replace the vote by an average: \(\hat y=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in N_k} y_i\), or a distance-weighted average. Everything else in this part carries over unchanged.

What it costs

Two ways to find the \(k\) smallest distances with a heap

Both approaches start from the \(m\) distances computed in step 1, at a cost of \(O(md)\).

Approach 1: a max-heap of size \(k\).

  1. Put the first \(k\) distances into a max-heap, so the root is the largest of the \(k\) kept so far.
  2. For each of the remaining \(m-k\) distances, compare it with the root. If it is smaller, remove the root and insert the new distance, at \(O(\log k)\) per replacement.
  3. At the end, the heap holds the \(k\) smallest distances.

That is \(m\) comparisons plus at most \(m\) replacements of \(O(\log k)\) each, giving \(O(m\log k)\) time and \(O(k)\) extra memory.

Approach 2: a min-heap of all \(m\) distances.

  1. Build a min-heap from all \(m\) distances with bottom-up heapify, which costs \(O(m)\), not \(O(m\log m)\).
  2. Extract the minimum \(k\) times, at \(O(\log m)\) each.

That gives \(O(m+k\log m)\) time. It uses \(O(m)\) memory, but the distance array already needs that.

$$\text{Approach 1: } O(m\log k)\qquad\qquad \text{Approach 2: } O(m+k\log m)$$

Which is better?

\(O(k\log m)\) on its own is the smaller term, but Approach 2 also pays \(O(m)\) to build the heap, so the fair comparison is \(m\log k\) against \(m+k\log m\). For \(3\le k\le m\),

$$k\log m\;\le\; m\log k,$$

because \(x/\log x\) increases for \(x>e\), so \(k\le m\) implies \(k/\log k\le m/\log m\). Adding the \(O(m)\) heapify cost does not change the ranking, since \(m\log k\) is already at least \(m\).

CaseApproach 1: \(m\log k\)Approach 2: \(m+k\log m\)
\(k\) constant (e.g. 5)\(O(m)\)\(O(m)\), a tie
\(k=\sqrt{m}\)\(O(m\log m)\)\(O(m)\), better
\(k=m\)\(O(m\log m)\)\(O(m\log m)\), a tie
\(m=10^6,\ k=10\)\(\approx 3.3\times10^{6}\)\(\approx 10^{6}\)

So Approach 2 is asymptotically at least as good, and strictly better when \(k\) grows with \(m\) but stays well below it.

Why Approach 1 is still common in practice

It needs only \(O(k)\) extra memory, and it works in a single pass while the distances are being computed, without storing them all. With \(k\) a small constant, as it usually is, it is just as fast as Approach 2.

Full cost of one prediction

Method for step 2Total time per query
Full sort (the lecture's algorithm)\(O(md+m\log m)\)
Approach 1: max-heap of size \(k\)\(O(md+m\log k)\)
Approach 2: min-heap of all \(m\)\(O(md+m+k\log m)=O(md+k\log m)\)

For small \(k\), both heap approaches reduce to \(O(md)\). Computing the distances is the real bottleneck either way.

PhaseTimeMemoryComment
Training\(O(1)\) beyond storing\(O(md)\)The whole dataset must be kept
Distances for one query\(O(md)\)\(O(m)\)One \(d\)-dimensional distance per training point
Finding the \(k\) smallest\(O(m\log m)\) by full sortOnly the \(k\) smallest are needed: a heap gives \(O(m\log k)\) or \(O(m+k\log m)\), quickselect \(O(m)\) on average
Training points (with labels) are \(A=(1,1)\,{+}\), \(B=(2,2)\,{+}\), \(E=(3,3.5)\,{-}\), \(F=(4,4.5)\,{-}\), \(G=(5,4)\,{-}\). Classify \(x_{\text{test}}=(3,2)\) with Euclidean distance for \(k=1,3,5\).
PointLabelSquared distanceDistanceRank
\(B\)+\(1^2+0^2=1\)1.0001
\(E\)−\(0^2+1.5^2=2.25\)1.5002
\(A\)+\(2^2+1^2=5\)2.2363
\(F\)−\(1^2+2.5^2=7.25\)2.6934
\(G\)−\(2^2+2^2=8\)2.8285

\(k=1\): only \(B\), so +. \(k=3\): \(B, E, A\) give two \(+\) against one \(-\), so +. \(k=5\): all five points, two \(+\) against three \(-\), so − — which is also simply the majority class of the training set, anticipating block 5. Note that ranking by squared distance gives the same order, so the square root never needs to be taken.

3

Measuring distance

"Nearest" means nothing until a distance is chosen, and the features are put on comparable scales.

Euclidean distance is common but not always right, and that different features may call for different metrics. The standard family is the Minkowski distance of order \(p\ge 1\):

$$d_p(x,z)=\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\lvert x_j-z_j\rvert^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p}$$
NameFormulaTypical use
Manhattan (\(p=1\))\(\sum_j \lvert x_j-z_j\rvert\)Grid-like movement; less dominated by one large difference
Euclidean (\(p=2\))\(\sqrt{\sum_j (x_j-z_j)^2}\)Continuous features on comparable scales — the default
Chebyshev (\(p\to\infty\))\(\max_j \lvert x_j-z_j\rvert\)When the single worst coordinate matters
Cosine distance\(1-\dfrac{x^{\top}z}{\lVert x\rVert\,\lVert z\rVert}\)Text and other data where direction matters more than length
Hamming\(\sum_j \mathbf{1}[x_j\ne z_j]\)Binary or categorical features

Feature scaling

This is the most important practical point about k-NN. Every distance above adds up raw differences across features, so a feature measured in large units swamps the others. Consider predicting whether a customer buys a product from age (years) and income (rupees):

PointAgeIncome (₹)Raw distance to testDistance after standardising
Test3050,000——
Neighbour \(P\)3158,000≈ 8,000\(\sqrt{0.1^2+0.4^2}\approx 0.41\)
Neighbour \(R\)5551,000≈ 1,000\(\sqrt{2.5^2+0.05^2}\approx 2.50\)

On raw values \(R\) is nearer, because a ₹1,000 gap outweighs a 25-year age gap. After dividing age by a standard deviation of 10 years and income by one of ₹20,000, \(P\) is clearly the nearer point — which matches intuition. The two standard rescalings are

$$\text{min–max: }\; x'_j=\frac{x_j-\min_j}{\max_j-\min_j}\in[0,1],\qquad \text{z-score: }\; x'_j=\frac{x_j-\mu_j}{\sigma_j}$$
Fit the scaling on training data only

The minimum, maximum, mean and standard deviation must be computed from the training set and then applied unchanged to validation and test points. Computing them on all the data lets information about the test set leak into the model.

For mixed data — some numeric, some categorical columns — no single metric fits every column. One option is to combine per-feature distances (range-normalised absolute difference for numeric columns, a 0/1 mismatch for categorical ones), which is the idea behind Gower's distance.

A dataset has 20 binary yes/no survey answers per respondent. Which distance is natural, and what does it count?

Hamming distance: the number of questions on which two respondents gave different answers. For 0/1 vectors it equals the Manhattan distance and also the squared Euclidean distance, so all three produce the same neighbour ranking.

4

k = 1: memorising the training set

The simplest version trusts a single neighbour completely, and inherits every one of its mistakes.

1-NN finds the single closest training point and copies its label. What could go wrong? Look at a region that is mostly green but contains one red point:

This is overfitting. With \(k=1\):

  • It is sensitive to outliers. If the nearest neighbour is mislabelled or noisy, the prediction is wrong — there is no second opinion.
  • It leaves holes in the decision boundary. Each outlier claims a region of its own.
  • Its training error is zero. Every training point is its own nearest neighbour at distance \(0\) (unless two identical inputs carry different labels). A perfect training score therefore says nothing about how 1-NN will do on new data.

The geometry of 1-NN

The region of space that is closer to training point \(x_i\) than to any other training point is called its Voronoi cell. 1-NN assigns every point in that cell the label \(y_i\), so the decision boundary is exactly the set of cell walls that separate points of different classes.

1-NN is not as bad as it sounds

A classical result (Cover and Hart, 1967) says that as the training set grows without limit, the error rate of 1-NN is at most twice the Bayes error — the error of the best possible classifier. So its weakness on finite, noisy data is variance, not a fundamental inability to learn the right boundary.

A 1-NN classifier scores 100% on its training set and 71% on a test set. Is something broken?

No. 100% training accuracy is guaranteed for 1-NN whenever no two identical inputs have different labels, so it carries no information. The 71% test accuracy is the only meaningful number, and the gap is the signature of overfitting — the remedy is a larger \(k\), chosen by cross-validation (block 6).

5

k = m: predicting the majority

At the other extreme, every point votes on every prediction, and location stops mattering.

If \(k=m\), the "\(k\) nearest neighbours" are the whole training set. The sum in the voting rule then runs over all \(m\) points no matter where \(x_{\text{test}}\) is, and it becomes the class count \(m_c\):

$$k=m:\qquad \hat y=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}[y_i=c]=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c}\; m_c$$

The prediction is the same constant — the most frequent class — for every input.

This is underfitting: the model ignores the input entirely. It is the opposite failure to block 4, where the model paid too much attention to individual points.

With \(k=m\), what accuracy does k-NN achieve on a test set drawn from the same distribution as a training set that is 75% class A?

About 75%: it always predicts A, so it is right exactly on the A examples. This "majority-class baseline" is the floor any real classifier must beat — a model scoring 75% on this data has learned nothing.

6

Choosing k

Between memorising and ignoring the data lies a useful range, and the only reliable way to find it is to test on data the model has not seen.

Small \(k\)Large \(k\)
Decision boundaryHighly complex and irregularOverly smooth
Reaction to noiseToo sensitive — every outlier mattersRobust, but may ignore genuine small structure
Training errorLow (zero at \(k=1\))High
Bias / varianceLow bias, high varianceHigh bias, low variance
Failure modeOverfitsUnderfits

Watching the boundary change

The two figures below use the same arrangement — a green central band between two red regions — but differ in how the noise is distributed.

Prefer odd k for two classes

With \(C=2\), any odd \(k\) makes a tied vote impossible. For \(C\) classes, avoiding values of \(k\) that are multiples of \(C\) removes the most common exact ties, but cannot rule out every one.

Cross-validation

The right \(k\) is usually found by cross-validation. The procedure, for \(K\)-fold cross-validation:

  1. Split the training data into \(K\) equal parts (folds), typically \(K=5\) or \(10\).
  2. For each candidate \(k\), and for each fold \(j\): use the other \(K-1\) folds as the stored training set, classify the points of fold \(j\), and record the error \(\mathrm{err}_j(k)\).
  3. Average: \(\mathrm{CV}(k)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathrm{err}_j(k)\).
  4. Choose \(k^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_k \mathrm{CV}(k)\), then use all the training data with that \(k\).
Round 1validatetraintraintraintrain
Round 2trainvalidatetraintraintrain
Round 3traintrainvalidatetraintrain
Round 4traintraintrainvalidatetrain
Round 5traintraintraintrainvalidate
Never tune k on the test set

Choosing \(k\) by test-set accuracy turns the test set into a second validation set, and the reported accuracy becomes optimistic. The test set is used once, after every choice has been made. A frequently quoted starting point is \(k\approx\sqrt{m}\), but it is only a rough heuristic to be checked by validation.

7

More than two classes

Nothing in the algorithm is specific to two classes: the vote simply has \(C\) candidates. The figure uses the Iris dataset with only two of its four features, sepal length and sepal width.

Plurality, not majority

With \(C\ge 3\) classes, the winning class may hold fewer than half the votes — for example 2 of \(k=5\) against 2 and 1. The rule is strictly a plurality vote (most votes wins), even though "majority voting" is the usual name.

8

The costs and limits of k-NN

Simple to state, expensive to run, and weaker than it looks once the number of features grows.

Issues:

  • Distance function choice. Euclidean is common but not always right, and different features may need different metrics (block 3).
  • Computational cost. Every prediction computes the distance from the test point to all \(m\) training points, so prediction time grows in proportion to the dataset size — \(O(md)\) per query. With billions of points this is prohibitive.
  • No actual learning. k-NN builds no model and extracts no structure. The entire dataset must be stored and consulted at prediction time, which is not memory-efficient.
Note:"

A single k-NN prediction is actually easy to explain — "these five most similar past cases were mostly positive" — and case-based explanations are used for exactly that reason. What k-NN lacks is a global summary: there are no weights or rules to inspect that describe the model as a whole. Decision trees (Part B) provide exactly that.

The curse of dimensionality

k-NN relies on "near" being meaningfully different from "far". In high dimensions that difference collapses: with points spread at random, the distance to the nearest point and the distance to the farthest point become almost equal.

Why the neighbourhood must grow: edges versus volume

Human brains are hardwired for three-dimensional space, so visualising 100 dimensions is impossible. To understand why a search box must expand so drastically just to capture 1% of the data, look at how adding dimensions changes the relationship between a shape's edges and its total volume. Throughout, assume the data is spread evenly and the goal is always to capture exactly 1% of it.

1 dimension: a line of string. A piece of string is 100 inches long, with data points spread evenly along it. To capture 1% of the data, cut off 1 inch. The search interval covers 1% of the string's length.

2 dimensions: a square sheet of paper. A sheet is 10 × 10 inches, or 100 square inches. Capturing 1% means capturing 1 square inch, which takes a 1 × 1 inch box. But 1 inch is 10% of the sheet's 10-inch width and 10% of its 10-inch height. To get 1% of the area, the search box has to stretch across 10% of each edge.

3 dimensions: a cube of cheese. A block is 10 × 10 × 10 inches, or 1,000 cubic inches. Capturing 1% means 10 cubic inches, which takes a smaller cube with sides of about 2.15 inches, since \(2.15^3\approx 10\). That is 21.5% of the block's length, width and height. To get 1% of the volume, the search box has to stretch across 21.5% of each edge.

The pattern

If a box covers a fraction \(s\) of every feature's range, it holds a fraction \(s^d\) of the total volume. To capture a fraction \(f\) of the data, the box therefore needs side

$$s^d=f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s=f^{1/d}$$
Dimensions \(d\)ExampleShare of each edge needed to capture 1%
1String\(0.01^{1/1}=1\%\)
2Sheet of paper\(0.01^{1/2}=10\%\)
3Block of cheese\(0.01^{1/3}\approx 21.5\%\)
10—\(0.01^{1/10}\approx 63\%\)
100—\(0.01^{1/100}\approx 95.5\%\)

As the dimension rises, the same 1% of the data forces a wider and wider net along every edge: 1%, then 10%, then 21.5%.

The 100-dimensional paradox

In 100 dimensions, small slices of the edges capture almost nothing. A search box covering 50% of every feature's range holds a fraction

$$0.5^{100}\approx 7.9\times 10^{-31}$$

of the space, which is practically zero, so it would catch no data points at all. To scrape together just 1% of the data, the box must satisfy \(0.955^{100}\approx 0.01\): it has to stretch across 95.5% of every single feature's range.

Why this breaks k-NN

The premise of k-nearest neighbours is that a prediction is based on a small, local group of similar points. In high dimensions, a group holding just 1% of the dataset needs a search box spanning 95.5% of the range of every feature. That is no longer a local neighbourhood of similar points. The net is so wide that it scoops up data from opposite ends of every feature's range, and the "nearest" neighbours are barely more similar to the test point than any other points.

Irrelevant features make this worse, since they add dimensions and distance without adding information. This is why feature selection or dimensionality reduction usually comes before k-NN.

Making it faster

  • Space-partitioning indexes such as k-d trees and ball trees avoid computing most distances. They work well in low dimensions and lose their advantage as \(d\) grows, for the reason just shown.
  • Approximate nearest-neighbour search (locality-sensitive hashing, graph-based indexes such as HNSW) returns neighbours that are very probably among the closest, at a small fraction of the cost. This is how large-scale similarity search is done in practice.
  • Reducing the stored set. Condensing removes points far from any boundary, which never change a prediction; editing removes points that disagree with their own neighbours, which are likely noise.
Strengths
  • No training phase; new data is added by storing it
  • Boundary of any shape; handles many classes naturally
  • Each prediction can be explained by its neighbours
  • Only one main hyperparameter, \(k\), plus the metric
Weaknesses
  • Slow, memory-hungry prediction
  • Needs feature scaling and a sensible metric
  • Degrades in high dimensions and with irrelevant features
  • No global model to inspect
Part B
Decision trees
9

From remembering to asking questions

k-NN keeps every training point. A decision tree compresses the data into a short sequence of yes/no questions.

One big disadvantage of k-NN is that it does not learn an underlying structure — it uses the input data exactly as it is. A decision tree tries to extract structure instead: it asks a series of questions about the features and routes each example down a path, so that many points which "mean the same thing" end up together in the same node.

TermMeaning
Root nodeThe first question; it receives all the training data
Internal (decision) nodeAny node that asks a question and has children
BranchOne possible answer to a node's question
Leaf nodeA node with no children; it outputs a class label
Depth of a nodeNumber of edges from the root to that node (the root has depth 0)
Height of a treeThe greatest depth of any leaf
Leaves are not always pure

The leaf nodes as pure nodes. That is the ideal, and it is what happens when a tree is grown until no more splitting is possible on clean data. But a leaf is also created when the depth limit is reached, when no attributes are left, or when no split improves purity (block 10). Such a leaf can contain a mixture of classes, and it then predicts the majority class among its training examples. Contradictory data — identical inputs with different labels — can never be split into pure leaves at all.

Compared with k-NN, a trained tree is compact and readable: every root-to-leaf path is an if–then rule, and prediction takes one comparison per level rather than one distance per training point.

10

How a tree grows

Split the data step by step on feature values, making each split as pure as possible, and stop when there is nothing left to gain.

  • Root node. Contains all the training data.
  • Splitting rule. Choose one feature and a threshold (or a value test) to divide the data.
  • Child nodes. Created by the split; each receives its own subset of the data.
  • Recursion. Repeat on each child until
    • the node is pure (all its samples belong to one class), or
    • the tree has reached a maximum depth, if one is set, or
    • no split improves the purity measure.

Questions on numeric features

For continuous features such as age, salary or temperature, a tree cannot create one branch per value. Instead, it splits the data into two branches using a threshold.

The splitting rule

For a numeric feature \(x_j\), the tree asks a yes/no question: is the value less than or equal to a threshold \(t\)? This divides the data \(D\) at the current node into two subsets:

$$D_{\text{left}}=\{(x,y)\in D : x_j\le t\}$$ $$D_{\text{right}}=\{(x,y)\in D : x_j> t\}$$
  • \(D_{\text{left}}\) contains every example whose value of \(x_j\) is less than or equal to \(t\). Values exactly equal to \(t\) go to this branch, by the convention explained in the note below.
  • \(D_{\text{right}}\) contains every example whose value of \(x_j\) is strictly greater than \(t\).
Where does a value equal to the threshold go?

The usual convention, and the one the later slides use ("Q ≤ threshold"), is that equality goes left.

The infinite-threshold problem

A threshold \(t\) can be any real number (5.1, 5.11, 5.111, …), so there are infinitely many candidates. But a node holds only finitely many examples, so testing every possible number is both impossible and unnecessary. Any threshold that falls strictly between the same two neighbouring data values produces exactly the same left/right split.

The midpoint solution

The tree therefore tests only a finite set of thresholds:

  1. Sort the values. Take the distinct values of \(x_j\) among the examples at the node and sort them: \(v_1<v_2<\dots<v_r\).
  2. Compute midpoints. For each consecutive pair, compute \(t=(v_i+v_{i+1})/2\).
  3. Test only those. With \(r\) distinct values there are exactly \(r-1\) midpoints, and every possible split of the node on \(x_j\) corresponds to one of them.
$$t_i=\frac{v_i+v_{i+1}}{2},\qquad i=1,2,\dots,r-1$$

Each candidate is scored with the purity measure of Part C, the reduction in Gini impurity or the information gain, and the best-scoring threshold is kept.

A worked example

A node contains three examples with ages 20, 24 and 30, so \(v_1=20\), \(v_2=24\), \(v_3=30\). Only two thresholds need testing:

$$t_1=\frac{20+24}{2}=22,\qquad t_2=\frac{24+30}{2}=27$$

To finish the example, suppose the labels are No, Yes, Yes. The parent node then has Gini impurity \(1-\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^2-\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2=\tfrac{4}{9}\approx 0.444\).

ThresholdLeft (age ≤ \(t\))Right (age > \(t\))Weighted Gini\(\Delta G\)
\(t_1=22\){20: No}, pure{24: Yes, 30: Yes}, pure\(0\)\(0.444\)
\(t_2=27\){20: No, 24: Yes}, \(G=0.5\){30: Yes}, pure\(\tfrac{2}{3}\times 0.5=0.333\)\(0.111\)

The tree chooses \(t_1=22\) and asks "is age ≤ 22?", because that split gives two pure children.

Keeping it fast

Sorting costs \(O(n\log n)\) for the \(n\) examples at the node. After that, all \(r-1\) thresholds can be scored in a single left-to-right sweep. Moving past each value shifts a few examples from the right child to the left, so the class counts, and hence the impurities, are updated in constant time per step instead of being recomputed from scratch.

Questions on categorical features

A categorical feature such as Outlook \(\in\{\text{Sunny},\text{Overcast},\text{Rain}\}\) can be split in two ways:

  • A multiway split creates one branch per value, as ID3 does.
  • A binary split asks a yes/no question such as "Outlook = Overcast?", as CART does.

What a tree does to the feature space

Every question on a single feature cuts the space with a line (in general, a hyperplane) parallel to one axis. A tree therefore divides the feature space into axis-aligned rectangles, one per leaf, each labelled with a class.

Once a tree is built: a feature's importance is measured as the total impurity reduction (Part C) produced by all the splits that use it, weighted by the number of samples reaching those splits.

11

A good question

A "good" question is one that

  • splits the data into purer subsets — closer to all-Yes or all-No, and
  • reduces uncertainty (impurity) as much as possible.

Counting Yes and No for each value of each feature makes the comparison concrete:

12

Two trees for the same data

Both trees below classify all 14 days correctly. One needs four questions; the other needs nine.

Starting with Outlook

Written with one branch per value, as ID3 builds it, the same tree is even smaller — three questions and five leaves:

Starting with Temperature

Both trees fit the training data perfectly, but the Temperature-first tree is more than twice as large, and its extra questions are fitted to one or two days each. Smaller trees that begin with informative questions are easier to read and usually generalise better — a preference known as Occam's razor, and the inductive bias that ID3's greedy choice builds in.

Part C
Measuring impurity
13

Three attribute selection measures

To pick the best question, we need a number for how mixed a node is, and a way to compare that number before and after a split.

Let a node contain examples from classes \(c=1,\dots,C\), and let \(p_c\) be the fraction of the node's examples in class \(c\). Three standard impurity measures are:

MeasureFormulaUsed by
Classification error\(H=1-\max_{c} p_c\)Rarely used for growing trees (block 14)
Gini index\(G=1-\sum_{c} p_c^{2}\)CART
Entropy\(E=-\sum_{c} p_c\log_2 p_c\)ID3, C4.5

All three are \(0\) for a pure node and largest when the classes are equally represented. In the entropy formula the term for an absent class is taken to be zero, by the convention \(0\log_2 0=0\) (justified by \(\lim_{p\to 0^+}p\log_2 p=0\)).

Scoring a split

  • A split sends the \(n\) examples of a parent node into children \(v\) with \(n_v\) examples each.
  • The impurity after the split is the size-weighted average of the children's impurities, and the quality of the split is how much that average falls below the parent's impurity:
$$\Delta I \;=\; {\color{#4A1E5C}{I(\text{parent})}} \;-\; \sum_{v} {\color{#1F8A85}{\frac{n_v}{n}}}\; {\color{#B23A6B}{I(\text{child}_v)}}$$
Before the splitImpurity of the node being split
WeightFraction of the parent's examples sent to child \(v\)
After the splitImpurity of each child

Here \(I\) is any of \(H\), \(G\) or \(E\), giving \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta G\) or \(\Delta E\). The best split is the one with the largest \(\Delta I\). With entropy, \(\Delta E\) has its own name: information gain. The next three blocks apply each measure to the same split.

14

Classification error and its blind spot

NodeClass fractionsClassification error \(H=1-\max_c p_c\)
Parent (15 A, 10 B)\(0.6,\ 0.4\)\(1-\tfrac{15}{25}=0.4\)
Left (5 A, 0 B)\(1,\ 0\)\(1-\tfrac{5}{5}=0\)
Right (10 A, 10 B)\(0.5,\ 0.5\)\(1-\tfrac{10}{20}=0.5\)

The weighted error after the split is

$$\frac{5}{25}\times 0+\frac{20}{25}\times 0.5=0.4 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Delta H=0.4-0.4=0$$

The split produced a pure node, so it clearly improved the data distribution — yet the classification error before and after is exactly the same. Classification error cannot see this improvement, and a tree grown with it might discard a useful split or stop early. This is why it is rarely used as the attribute selection measure; the next two measures capture the improvement.

Why the improvement vanishes

Suppose class A is the majority in the parent and also in every child (for the 10/10 child, either class may be taken as the majority; choose A). Then each child's error is \(1-n_{v,A}/n_v\), where \(n_{v,A}\) is the number of A examples in child \(v\), and

$$\sum_v \frac{n_v}{n}\left(1-\frac{n_{v,A}}{n_v}\right)=1-\frac{\sum_v n_{v,A}}{n}=1-\frac{n_A}{n}=H(\text{parent})$$

So whenever a split leaves the majority class unchanged in every child, \(\Delta H=0\), however much purer the children become. Classification error only rewards splits that change which class is predicted somewhere. Geometrically, \(H\) is made of straight line segments (block 17), and a weighted average of points on one straight segment lies on that same segment.

Keep the parent (15 A, 10 B) but split it into (3 A, 8 B) and (12 A, 2 B). What is \(\Delta H\) now?

Left child error \(1-\tfrac{8}{11}=\tfrac{3}{11}\); right child error \(1-\tfrac{12}{14}=\tfrac{2}{14}\). Weighted: \(\tfrac{11}{25}\cdot\tfrac{3}{11}+\tfrac{14}{25}\cdot\tfrac{2}{14}=\tfrac{3}{25}+\tfrac{2}{25}=0.2\). So \(\Delta H=0.4-0.2=0.2>0\). Classification error does register this split, because the left child's majority has changed to B.

15

Gini index

$$G=1-\sum_{c}p_c^{2}$$ $$\text{two classes:}\quad G=1-p^2-(1-p)^2=2p(1-p)$$

A useful reading: if two examples are drawn at random, with replacement, from the node, \(\sum_c p_c^2\) is the probability that they have the same class, so \(G\) is the probability that they differ. Equivalently, it is the error rate of a classifier that guesses labels at random in proportion to the node's class frequencies.

Applied to the same split:

Node\(P(A)\)\(P(B)\)Gini
Parent\(\tfrac{15}{25}=0.6\)\(\tfrac{10}{25}=0.4\)\(1-(0.6^2+0.4^2)=1-0.52=0.48\)
Left\(\tfrac{5}{5}=1\)\(\tfrac{0}{5}=0\)\(1-(1^2+0^2)=0\)
Right\(\tfrac{10}{20}=0.5\)\(\tfrac{10}{20}=0.5\)\(1-(0.5^2+0.5^2)=0.5\)
$$G_{\text{split}}=\frac{5}{25}\times 0+\frac{20}{25}\times 0.5=0.4,\qquad \Delta G=0.48-0.4=0.08$$

The improvement in Gini index is the parent Gini minus the weighted Gini of the children, \(0.08>0\). The Gini index captures the improvement that classification error missed.

16

Entropy and information gain

$$E=-\sum_{c}p_c\log_2 p_c$$ $$\text{two classes:}\quad E=-p\log_2 p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$$

Entropy measures uncertainty in bits: the average number of yes/no questions needed to identify the class of an example drawn from the node, using an optimal code. A 50/50 binary node needs a full bit; a pure node needs none.

For the parent, \(\log_2 0.6\approx -0.737\) and \(\log_2 0.4\approx -1.322\), so

$$E_{\text{parent}}=-\bigl(0.6\times(-0.737)+0.4\times(-1.322)\bigr)=0.442+0.529=0.971$$
NodeEntropy
Parent (0.6, 0.4)\(0.971\)
Left (1, 0)\(-\bigl(1\cdot\log_2 1+0\cdot\log_2 0\bigr)=0\)
Right (0.5, 0.5)\(-\bigl(0.5\log_2 0.5+0.5\log_2 0.5\bigr)=-\bigl(0.5(-1)+0.5(-1)\bigr)=1\)

The weighted entropy of the children is \(\frac{5}{25}\times 0+\frac{20}{25}\times 1=0.8\), and the information gain is the parent entropy minus that:

$$\mathrm{IG}(D,A)=E(D)-\sum_{v\in\text{values}(A)}\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}\,E(D_v)$$ $$\mathrm{IG}=0.971-0.8=0.171$$

Like Gini, information gain registers the improvement from the split. Information gain is also the mutual information between the attribute and the class label: how many bits of uncertainty about the label are removed, on average, by learning the attribute's value.

Why is information gain never negative?

Entropy is a concave function of the class distribution, and the parent's distribution is exactly the weighted average of the children's distributions (with weights \(n_v/n\)). By Jensen's inequality, the entropy of an average is at least the average of the entropies, so \(E(\text{parent})\ge\sum_v \frac{n_v}{n}E(\text{child}_v)\). Equality holds only when every child has the same class distribution as the parent. The same argument applies to Gini, and to classification error — which is why \(\Delta H\ge 0\) too, even though it is often exactly \(0\).

17

Comparing the three measures

Reading the plot

The horizontal axis is labelled "purity", but it is actually \(p\), the fraction of examples in one of the two classes. Purity is highest at both ends of the axis (\(p=0\) and \(p=1\)) and lowest in the middle. Also, the plot writes classification error as \(E(t)\), which clashes with \(E\) for entropy; these notes use \(H\) throughout.

Ranges

For two classes, \(E\in[0,1]\), \(G\in[0,0.5]\) and \(H\in[0,0.5]\). The same logic extends to multi-class classification. Every measure is maximised when all \(C\) classes are equally likely, \(p_c=1/C\), which gives:

MeasureMaximum at \(p_c=1/C\)Range\(C=2\)\(C=4\)
Classification error\(1-\tfrac{1}{C}\)\(\bigl[0,\ 1-\tfrac{1}{C}\bigr]\)\(0.5\)\(0.75\)
Gini index\(1-C\cdot\tfrac{1}{C^2}=1-\tfrac{1}{C}\)\(\bigl[0,\ 1-\tfrac{1}{C}\bigr]\)\(0.5\)\(0.75\)
Entropy\(-C\cdot\tfrac{1}{C}\log_2\tfrac{1}{C}=\log_2 C\)\(\bigl[0,\ \log_2 C\bigr]\)\(1\)\(2\)

Is ΔE ≥ ΔG ≥ ΔH?

For a split, the improvement in entropy is at least the improvement in Gini, which is at least the improvement in classification error. For the example of blocks 14–16 this holds: \(0.171\ge 0.08\ge 0\). As a general rule, only half of it is true.

What is always true is the ordering of the impurities themselves, at every class distribution:

$$E\;\ge\; G\;\ge\; H$$

since \(\sum_c p_c^2\le \max_c p_c\sum_c p_c=\max_c p_c\) gives \(G\ge H\), and \(-\log_2 p_c\ge 1-p_c\) for every \(p_c\in(0,1]\) gives \(E\ge G\). The first half of the slide's chain, \(\Delta E\ge\Delta G\), also holds for every split: the difference \(E-G\) is itself a concave function of the class distribution, so by the Jensen argument of block 16 its improvement \(\Delta E-\Delta G\) is non-negative.

Note: ΔG ≥ ΔH is not a general rule

Take a balanced parent with 10 A and 10 B, and split it into two children of 10 examples each, one with 6 A and 4 B, the other with 4 A and 6 B.

MeasureParentEach childImprovement
Entropy1.0000.971\(\Delta E=0.029\)
Gini0.5000.480\(\Delta G=0.020\)
Classification error0.5000.400\(\Delta H=0.100\)

Here \(\Delta H>\Delta E>\Delta G\). Classification error has a sharp corner at \(p=0.5\), so a split whose children land on opposite sides of that corner is rewarded heavily. The accurate statement is: \(\Delta E\ge\Delta G\) always; \(\Delta E\) and \(\Delta G\) are strictly positive whenever the children's class distributions differ from the parent's; \(\Delta H\) can be \(0\) in exactly those cases (block 14), but is not always the smallest of the three.

Comparing raw \(\Delta\) values across measures is not very meaningful anyway, since entropy runs on roughly twice the scale of Gini. What matters when growing a tree is how one measure ranks the candidate splits at a node. Gini and entropy rarely disagree about that ranking; Gini is slightly cheaper because it needs no logarithms.

Part D
Building and trusting trees
18

Worked example: ID3 on PlayTennis

Block 11 argued that Outlook is the best first question. Information gain confirms it, and then builds the rest of the tree.

Entropy at the root

The root holds all 14 days: 9 Yes and 5 No.

$$E(S)=-\frac{9}{14}\log_2\frac{9}{14}-\frac{5}{14}\log_2\frac{5}{14}=0.410+0.530=0.940$$

Gain for Outlook

Outlook splits the 14 days into Sunny [2 Yes, 3 No], Overcast [4 Yes, 0 No] and Rain [3 Yes, 2 No]. A 2–3 or 3–2 split has entropy \(0.971\) (the same value as block 16, since \(\{0.4, 0.6\}\) is the same pair of fractions), and a pure node has \(0\):

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{IG}(S,\text{Outlook})&=0.940-\Bigl(\tfrac{5}{14}\times 0.971+\tfrac{4}{14}\times 0+\tfrac{5}{14}\times 0.971\Bigr)\\&=0.940-0.694=0.246\end{aligned}$$

Using Gini instead of entropy, which attribute would CART-style scoring put at the root of PlayTennis?

The Gini improvements for multiway splits on the four attributes are Outlook \(0.116\), Humidity \(0.092\), Wind \(0.031\), Temperature \(0.019\). (CART itself would ask binary questions such as "Outlook = Overcast?", but the conclusion about which attribute matters most is the same.)

19

The ID3 algorithm and its relatives

DecisionTree(\(D\), Attributes)
  1. If all examples in \(D\) belong to the same class, return a leaf with that class.
  2. If Attributes is empty, return a leaf with the majority class in \(D\).
  3. For each attribute \(A\) in Attributes, compute AttributeSelectionMeasure(\(A\)) on \(D\) — for example information gain or Gini reduction.
  4. Let \(A_{\text{best}}\) be the attribute with the best score (highest information gain or highest Gini reduction).
  5. Create a decision node that splits on \(A_{\text{best}}\).
  6. For each possible value \(v\) of \(A_{\text{best}}\):
    1. Let \(D_v\) be the examples in \(D\) with \(A_{\text{best}}=v\).
    2. If \(D_v\) is empty, attach a leaf labelled with the majority class in \(D\); otherwise attach the subtree DecisionTree(\(D_v\), Attributes \(\setminus\{A_{\text{best}}\}\)).
  7. Return the constructed tree.

A few points about this procedure:

  • It is greedy. Each node takes the locally best attribute and never revisits the choice. The result is usually good but not guaranteed to be the smallest consistent tree; finding that tree exactly is NP-complete.
  • Empty branches (step 6b) happen when some value of \(A_{\text{best}}\) never occurs among the examples at this node. The parent's majority class is the best available guess.
  • A categorical attribute is used at most once per path, because every example below it shares one value. A numeric attribute can be reused with different thresholds, so implementations for numeric data do not remove it from the list.
  • The slides' third stopping rule (block 10), "no improvement after the split", is not in this pseudocode. Adding "if the best score is \(0\), or below a small threshold, return a majority leaf" gives it. Block 20 shows why that rule must be used with care.

ID3, C4.5 and CART

ID3C4.5CART
Full nameIterative Dichotomiser 3Successor to ID3Classification and Regression Trees
CriterionInformation gain (entropy)Gain ratioGini index (classification); variance (regression)
SplitsMultiway, one branch per valueMultiway; thresholds for numeric featuresAlways binary
FeaturesCategoricalCategorical and numeric, missing valuesCategorical and numeric
PruningNoneError-based post-pruningCost-complexity pruning

The bias of information gain

Information gain favours attributes with many values. PlayTennis shows this dramatically if the Day column is treated as an attribute: every day is unique, so splitting on Day produces 14 pure leaves and

$$\mathrm{IG}(S,\text{Day})=0.940-0=0.940$$

— the largest possible gain, and a completely useless tree that cannot classify any new day. C4.5 penalises such splits by dividing by the split information, the entropy of the partition itself:

$$\mathrm{SplitInfo}(D,A)=-\sum_{v}\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}\log_2\frac{|D_v|}{|D|}$$ $$\mathrm{GainRatio}(D,A)=\frac{\mathrm{IG}(D,A)}{\mathrm{SplitInfo}(D,A)}$$
AttributeIGSplitInfoGain ratio
Day0.940\(\log_2 14=3.807\)0.247
Outlook0.2461.5770.156
Humidity0.1511.0000.152
Wind0.0480.9850.049
Temperature0.0291.5570.019
Gain ratio reduces the bias; it does not remove it

Day's gain ratio (0.247) still beats Outlook's (0.156) here, so gain ratio alone would still choose the identifier. Identifiers such as a row number, a date or a customer ID carry no information that generalises and should be dropped before training. Gain ratio is designed for the milder case of genuine attributes with different numbers of values.

Trees for regression

The "R" in CART: when \(y\) is numeric, a leaf predicts the mean of its examples, and impurity is measured by variance. The best split maximises the variance reduction \(\operatorname{Var}(D)-\sum_v \frac{|D_v|}{|D|}\operatorname{Var}(D_v)\) — the same \(\Delta I\) as block 13 with \(I=\operatorname{Var}\).

20

Can ID3 produce more than one tree?

The lecture's food for thought: can ID3 generate multiple decision trees for the same dataset, when does that happen, and must those trees have the same height?

Consider eight examples with three binary attributes:

ABCY
000P
001P
010Q
011Q
100Q
101Q
110P
111P

The label is \(Y=P\) exactly when \(A=B\) — an XNOR of \(A\) and \(B\) — and \(C\) is irrelevant. At the root, the information gains of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are equal, so any of them may be chosen first.

They are equal because they are all zero

Splitting on any one attribute leaves 2 P and 2 Q on each side, the same 50/50 mix as the root, so \(\mathrm{IG}(A)=\mathrm{IG}(B)=\mathrm{IG}(C)=1-1=0\). No single attribute says anything about \(Y\) on its own; only the combination of \(A\) and \(B\) does. This has a sharp consequence: an implementation that stops when the best gain is zero (block 19) would stop at the root and return a leaf, although a height-2 tree classifies every example perfectly. Greedy, one-attribute-at-a-time scoring is blind to interactions like XOR.

Split on A first

Split on B first

Split on C first

After splitting on C, each child again holds 2 P and 2 Q, and now A and B both have information gain \(0\) within it — another tie. Either can be chosen next, and only then does the remaining attribute separate the classes.

Answers

Can ID3 generate multiple decision trees for the same dataset?

Yes. ID3 is deterministic except when it has to break a tie, and the dataset above produces four different trees depending on how its ties are broken.

What must hold for that to happen, and what is enough?

Necessary: at some node that ID3 actually reaches, two or more attributes tie for the highest information gain. Without such a tie, every choice is forced and the tree is unique.

Sufficient: such a tie exists, and the tie-break can go either way. Choosing a different attribute at that node gives a tree that tests a different attribute there — a different tree.

The slides add a condition to the necessary part: that none of the tied attributes leads to immediate termination at that node. That condition cannot be necessary while the plain tie is sufficient, since a sufficient condition must imply every necessary one. The added condition matters for a narrower question: whether the resulting trees can differ in shape. If each tied attribute immediately splits the node into pure leaves, the alternative trees differ only in which attribute is tested at that node, with the same size and height.

If ID3 can generate multiple trees, must they have the same height?

No. Splitting on A or B first gives height 2; splitting on C first gives height 3. The C-first trees are also twice as large and test an attribute that has no bearing on the label. Both of their subtrees are identical, which means the test on C can be removed without changing any prediction — exactly the kind of simplification that pruning (block 21) looks for.

21

Overfitting and pruning

A tree grown until every leaf is pure has memorised its training set, exactly as 1-NN does.

Without a stopping rule, splitting continues until each leaf is pure, which means zero training error whenever the data has no contradictory duplicates. The last panel of the figure in block 10 shows the result: tiny rectangles fitted around individual noisy points. Depth plays the role for trees that \(k\) plays for k-NN, in the opposite direction — a larger \(k\) is simpler, a larger depth is more complex.

Pre-pruning: stop early

Stop splitting a node when a limit is reached:

  • a maximum depth;
  • a minimum number of samples required to split a node, or to form a leaf;
  • a minimum impurity decrease — the "no metric improvement" rule of block 10 with a threshold above zero.

Pre-pruning is cheap, but it can stop too soon: a split that looks worthless may enable valuable splits below it, as the XOR example of block 20 shows.

Post-pruning: grow, then cut back

Grow the full tree, then replace subtrees by leaves when that does not hurt performance on held-out data. Reduced-error pruning removes a subtree whenever validation accuracy does not drop. CART's cost-complexity pruning balances fit against size:

$$R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha\,\lvert \mathrm{leaves}(T)\rvert$$

Here \(R(T)\) is the training error of tree \(T\) and \(\alpha\ge 0\) is the price of each leaf. Increasing \(\alpha\) gives a sequence of ever smaller trees; cross-validation picks the \(\alpha\) — just as it picks \(k\) in block 6.

Beyond single trees

Single trees have high variance: a small change in the data can change the root split and everything below it. Ensembles average that variance away. A random forest trains many trees on bootstrap samples, with a random subset of features considered at each split, and takes a vote; gradient boosting builds shallow trees one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.

Strengths of decision trees
  • Readable if–then rules and feature importances
  • No feature scaling needed; mixed feature types are fine
  • Fast prediction: one comparison per level
  • Irrelevant features tend to be ignored
Weaknesses of decision trees
  • Overfit easily without pruning
  • Unstable: small data changes can change the whole tree
  • Axis-aligned cuts approximate diagonal boundaries poorly
  • Greedy growth misses interactions like XOR
22

k-NN and decision trees side by side

k-nearest neighboursDecision tree
What is learnedNothing; the data is storedA hierarchy of feature tests
Training costNone beyond storageRoughly \(O(d\,m\log m)\) per level for numeric features
Prediction cost\(O(md)\) per query\(O(\text{height})\) per query
MemoryThe whole datasetThe tree only
Decision boundaryPiecewise linear, any orientationAxis-aligned rectangles
Feature scalingEssentialNot needed
Irrelevant featuresHurt every distanceUsually never selected
Complexity knob\(k\): small overfits, large underfitsDepth / pruning: deep overfits, shallow underfits
ExplanationPer prediction: "these neighbours"Global: readable rules
Extreme setting\(k=1\): zero training error; \(k=m\): majority classFull depth: zero training error; depth 0: majority class
A dataset has 50 numeric features, of which only 3 matter, and the features are in wildly different units. Which of the two methods is the safer first choice, and why?

A decision tree. Its splits compare one feature against a threshold, so units never interact and no scaling is needed, and the 47 irrelevant features are unlikely to be chosen if the 3 useful ones carry the signal. k-NN would need careful scaling, and even then the 47 irrelevant dimensions would add noise to every distance and push the data into the regime of block 8 where nearest neighbours stop being meaningfully near.

The true class boundary is the diagonal line \(x_1=x_2\). Which method approximates it more economically?

k-NN. Its boundary can run in any direction, so with enough data it follows the diagonal directly. A tree must build the diagonal as a staircase of horizontal and vertical cuts, and needs more and more leaves to make the steps small. (Adding the feature \(x_1-x_2\) would let a tree solve it with a single split.)
